title: Delhi AQI Hits 451 as Purifier Costs Put Clean Indoor Air Out of Reach
excerpt: As the capital's air enters the severe zone ahead of Diwali, residents say the machines, filters and systems sold as protection are priced beyond most households — and doctors warn even a purifier is no guarantee.
body:
• Delhi's air quality index reached 451 on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, pushing the capital into the severe category, according to Herzindagi's report on the day's readings.
  • Residents are rushing to buy air purifiers, but even sale-season prices — from about Rs 4,499 for a small-room unit to Rs 14,160 for a large-room model — put effective protection beyond many households, The Hindu reported.
  • Doctors warn a purifier is not a guarantee: former AIIMS director Dr Randeep Guleria says purifiers have not been conclusively proven to protect against Delhi's toxic air, and a tightly fitted mask offers some protection outdoors.
  • For families visiting Delhi for Diwali, the practical steps are a sealed, well-fitted mask outside, one closed room with a correctly sized HEPA purifier inside, and daily AQI checks before children play outdoors.

Delhi's air turned toxic again this week, and the city's annual scramble for protection ran into a familiar wall: price. The Hindu reported that as New Delhi's air quality deteriorated, residents complained that air purification products — the machines, replacement filters and whole-home systems now marketed as essential household equipment — are unaffordable for most families. Herzindagi reported that Delhi's air quality index reached 451 on Tuesday, November 3, putting the capital in the severe zone as Diwali approaches.

The complaint is not that purifiers do not exist. It is that protection has become a consumer purchase, priced like one. Retail listings tracked during Flipkart's Big Bang Diwali Sale, which began on October 28, show the spread: a Motorola AirShield 150 for small rooms at Rs 4,499, a Honeywell Air Touch V1 at Rs 5,149, a Philips model at Rs 9,499, a Mi Smart Air Purifier 4 Lite at Rs 10,990, and a large-room CUCKOO Respure unit at Rs 14,160, according to Herzindagi's sale roundup. Those are discounted prices, before replacement filters and electricity, and each machine cleans one enclosed room — not a home, and not the street outside.

Even a Purchased Purifier Has Limits

Doctors caution that buying the machine does not settle the health question. Dr Randeep Guleria, the former director of AIIMS who now chairs the Institute of Internal Medicine and Respiratory and Sleep Medicine at Medanta, told CNN that air purifiers have not been conclusively proven to protect people from Delhi's toxic air, as reported by World News 24x7. A purifier's effectiveness depends on the size of the room and whether doors and windows stay shut; polluted air keeps entering through open doors, and a unit placed at one end of a large room may not clean the air throughout it.

"A person who dies of dengue or swine flu is recorded as such, but a death certificate does not say the person died of pollution."

— Dr Randeep Guleria, former AIIMS director

Guleria described air pollution as a "silent killer" whose impact goes unrecorded because pollution is rarely listed as a direct cause of death, and he warned that children growing up in highly polluted environments risk impaired lung development. Research he cited found that children raised amid high pollution can develop lower lung function than children in cleaner air — though a follow-up study in the United States found children's lung function improved after air quality improved. He said a properly fitted mask that seals around the nose and mouth can provide some protection on poor-air days.

Why This November Is Worse Than a Bad Week

Delhi's deterioration follows a pattern our coverage has tracked through the season: farm fires have fallen sharply this year, yet the capital's air still turned 'very poor' at AQI 324 earlier in the cycle, and winter pollution curbs — including a vehicle ban and 50 percent work from home — have begun. The gap between those two facts is the story residents are living: the sources regulators can count are shrinking, while the air readers breathe is not improving at the same pace, and the cost of adapting is being transferred to households one appliance at a time. Related coverage: farm fires fall, but Delhi's air turns 'very poor' and Delhi's winter pollution curbs begin.

What Households Can Do Now

The measures with evidence behind them are unglamorous. Keep one room closed and run a correctly sized purifier in it — Herzindagi's listings show why sizing matters, with coverage ranging from 190 square feet for the cheapest unit to 570 square feet for the largest. Wear a tightly fitted mask outdoors on severe days, per Guleria's advice. Check the AQI before sending children out to play. Guleria argued the lasting fix is policy, not retail: he called for clear annual targets to bring AQI down by a defined number of points, and said cities including London, Los Angeles and Beijing show sustained action can deliver meaningful improvement within five to 10 years. Until then, clean indoor air in Delhi remains something families buy by the room — if they can buy it at all.
